nodes.question: What limitation do current LCA standards, EN 15804(2012) + A2(2019), have regarding emissions?
nodes.answer: They do not take into account the timing of when emissions occur.
nodes.paragraph: (2022a, b) developed GWP100 ranges. Carcassi et al. (2022) based their work on a specific (bamboo) product and developed three end-of-life scenarios for a novel mycelium insulation. The uniqueness of the study was to implement a dynamic LCIA that accounts for the growth and cultivation of bamboo used for the insulation manufacturing. However, the focus of Cascione et al. (2022a, b) and Carcassi et al. (2022) is limited to greenhouse emissions. Other emissions as listed in EN (2012) were not explored. Current LCA standards, EN 15804(2012) + A2(2019), do not take into account the timing for when emissions occur. Therefore, the temporary sequestration of carbon in bio-based materials and the temporary reduction of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere are not considered. Similar to Hawkins et al. (2021), Carcassi et al. (2022) presented a dynamic LCIA that considers the timings of green-house emissions. Dynamic life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) is an approach that investigates time-dependent environmental impacts (Levasseur n.d.).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Energy-efficient appliances|Life-cycle analysis of appliances_qna_001
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What types of products have most LCA literature reviews focused on?
nodes.answer: Most LCA literature reviews have focused on consumer electronics.
nodes.paragraph: 2018). Life cycle assessment (LCA) is an internationally standardised method to quantify the potential environmental impacts of products by taking into consideration the full life cycle of the product (ISO 14040, 2006). Several literature reviews have been conducted in the field of LCA of electronic products (Ghisellini et al. 2023; Andrae 2016; Teixeira et al. 2020; Nunes et al. 2021; Sub- ramanian and Yung 2016; He et al. 2023). Most of these reviews focus on consumer electronics. Some reviews have been conducted in specific areas of healthcare, such as environmental sustainability of mobile health technolo- gies (Dekimpe et al. 2022), comparison of single-use and reusable healthcare devices and products (Keil et al. 2022; S rensen et al. 2022), pharma-LCAs (Yang et al. 2020; De Soete et al. 2014), and environmental sustainability of surgi - cal procedures (Papadopoulou et al. 2022). However, to our knowledge, there is no review focused on EHDs yet. Also, LCA studies of EHDs used to conduct surgery (electronic surgical devices) are rarely addressed in the literature.

Moreover, the impacts of these devices are mostly considered at the product level and overlook potential indirect impacts associated with the healthcare value delivered by the EHDs (e.g. fewer hospital bed days). Conclusions It is important to consider a wider boundary of healthcare pathway rather than the narrow boundary of the device. This will involve considering both the direct life cycle impacts of the device (e.g. impacts related to production or end-of-life) and the positive and negative effects of using the EHDs at the healthcare pathway level. nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do rented garments compare to owned garments in terms of greenhouse gas emissions according to the LCA?
nodes.answer: According to the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), rented garments have a greater life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) per piece when dry-cleaned compared to owned garments. However, the GHG emissions per wear are significantly reduced for rented garments that increase lifetime wear, such as dresses.

nodes.answer: Ncube et al. (2022) were able to carry out comparative assessments between linear and circular production, leading to the definition of proper circular strategies to reduce environmental footprints.

In recent years, several studies have shown the positive inter - action between LCA and circular economy. By applying the LCA methodology in the construction industry, Honar - var et al. (2022) showed an increase in circularity of 27% in old buildings and 3% in new ones due to the adoption of biocompatible materials and regenerative design. Like- wise, Bj rnbet and Vild sen S (2021) study on a Norwegian manufacturer revealed that LCA is a suitable methodology for the development of circular business models as it pro- vides quantified results about the environmental impacts of circular strategies, limiting the risk of problem shifting and considering multiple environmental impact categories. On the other hand, the use of the LCA method enabled Ncube et al. (2022) to carry out comparative assessments between linear and circular production within the supply chain of Italian extra virgin olive oil, leading to the definition of proper circular strategies to reduce environmental footprints in this sector.

nodes.question: What is a major consequence of using estimates or excluding steps in the production process within the LCA methodology?
nodes.answer: The major consequence is the compromise of assessment accuracy, which can increase variability and uncertainty in the results of the analysis.
nodes.paragraph: However, the LCA methodology presents relevant chal- lenges that may affect its application in business contexts (Testa et al. 2016; Sassanelli et al. 2019) and in circular practices (Toniolo et al. 2023). These include the difficulty of collecting reliable and accurate data needed to ensure traceability and transparency of the analysis (Saberi et al. 2019; Sassanelli et al. 2019; Carri res et al. 2021). nodes.answer: The development of high-resolution data allows for the calculation of GHG emissions of individual finishing cattle, which represents a novel approach in Life Cycle Inventory analysis.
nodes.paragraph: The sophistication of LCA has evolved rapidly in recent years (e.g. McLaren et al. 2021) and arguably has become the de facto gold standard means to quantify environmental footprints of agri-food commodity supply chains in silico over the last few decades (lgos et al. 2019 ). Indeed, one such example of advancing LCA is how high-resolution data can catapult the method through the development of a novel approach to life cycle inventory analysis (LCI) by calculating GHG emissions of individual finishing cattle thus enabling the assessment of dependent (emissions) and independent variables (e.g. growth rates, breeds, and sex) to identify the most promising areas in terms of livestock management and GHG mitigation. nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What must LCA studies acknowledge to ensure scientific robustness according to the consensus mentioned?
nodes.answer: LCA studies must acknowledge uncertainties inherent within production systems.
nodes.paragraph: 2020). Additionally, there is now a consensus that LCA stud- ies must acknowledge uncertainties inherent within pro- duction systems to ensure their scientific robustness (lgos et al. 2019). Theoretically speaking, uncertainties in carbon footprint estimates can arise from either of the two compu- tational stages of LCA, namely, life cycle inventory analysis (LCI) and life cycle impact assessment (LCIA). Within the context of livestock production systems, however, the choice of LCIA methodology has been shown to impart negligible effects on global warming potential as long as the timescale of analysis (e.g. 20 years, 100 years, or 500 years) is clearly defined (Reckmann 2013). Uncertainties associated with LCI, on the other hand, have considerable impacts on envi- ronmental footprints arising from different farming systems (McAuliffe et al. 2017) and are also of relevance to a large population of practitioners around the world.
